title: Retirement scheme crackdown looms
full_text:
The nation's largest wealth managers are bracing for a potential government crackdown on retirement products engineered to artificially trim superannuation balances to max out a member's aged pension entitlements.
Widely labelled as "pension bonus" or "boost" products, these strategies have become popular and represent more than $21.5 billion of funds under management at big retail super powerhouses including AMP, MLC and Colonial First State, where they have been used to poach industry fund members as they near retirement.
It is a part of the market that has come under scrutiny over the past year. Statistics consistently show billions of dollars in outflows from industry funds that are losing members to newer investment platforms run by the retail funds.
Competitors have rounded on the products, saying they encourage people to double-dip on the aged pension at a cost to taxpayers.
Many of the benefits in the products are not portable — if members switch funds they will lose the accrued advantages, which discourages them from changing superannuation provider.
Treasury is examining the rules surrounding the products and has talked to various industry figures before a broader consultation on their future, according to three sources with knowledge of the discussions who commented anonymously to protect their relationship with the department.
Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia chief executive Mary Delahunty said the funds had acted "entirely appropriately" and had previously been encouraged by the government to pursue these sorts of retirement products following changes to superannuation laws in 2017.
"They were given some leeway to use the existing rules as they are written to maximise their members' income in retirement," she said. "This is not an example of funds gaming the rules for their own gain. This is to benefit their members, and it is no surprise the products have been popular with them."
There were fears about what, if any, constraints on the products may be introduced, Delahunty said.
Any major changes are likely to upend competitive strategies for funds that have leaned hard into them.
Adding to the anxiety within the sector has been the department's repeated assurances that a much broader consultation on the issue would begin within a week or two - a self-imposed deadline that Treasury has consistently missed despite talking to the sector since early September.
David Bell, executive director at retirement think tank the Conexus Institute, said it was important for any review to consider portability and access to such schemes for a broader range of unadvised super members.
While "admiring many of the benefits that these products can provide", he said there was a need to examine if the pension incentives went too far.
The products optimise retirement rules by guaranteeing income for life and unlocking favourable age pension means test concessions.
For example, only 60 per cent of the gross income received from a boost product is counted as assessable income by Centrelink, and AMP promotes that retirees could receive $100,000 more in the first 10 years of retirement.
Bell said the sizeable take-up of boost products meant it was important for the government to review the settings.
He said the industry would also benefit from a clearer policy. "Providing certainty will increase offerings by super funds and likely take-up. We think there is opportunity for a balanced calibration around age, deeming rates and perhaps a cap."
A spokesperson for Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the department had "had some good discussions with the super sector about the retirement phase and we've publicly flagged we'll work closely with them to get retirement products and information-sharing right".
The future of these products, and the $4.8 trillion sector's need to meet a so-called grey tsunami of retirees and drawdowns after 30 years of accumulation, will be a major talking point at the Financial Review Super and Wealth Summit in Melbourne on Monday.
AMP retirement executive Ben Hillier will discuss retirement income and financial advice on a panel at the event, though the company declined to comment on Sunday.
One of the summit's main topics will be the sector's need to evolve beyond its focus on accumulation to meet the needs of the 1.7 million Australians who intend to retire over the coming decade.
Government reviews have found that retirees do not use their superannuation savings effectively, drawing down only the minimum and dying with the bulk of their wealth intact.
It is also an area of intense interest for the Australian Securities and Investments Commission and Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, which have published critical updates on the sector's progress.
The regulators jointly noted the poor level of retirement support in a review last year of the sector's retirement income obligations, saying the gap between the best and worst funds in this regard was widening.
"Unless action is taken, particularly by those falling behind, the quality of support provided to members approaching or in retirement, and the outcomes delivered to members in retirement will be impacted," they said.
Delahunty said the work on boost and similar products that fall under a category called "innovative retirement income streams" was progressing across several retail and industry super funds. "The products in the market are geared towards financial advisers, so that is naturally more on the retail funds side, but all the super funds I have spoken to over the last 12 months are working on their retirement solutions in a way that matches their member cohort," she said.
